chunks: Fourier Transform vs Fourier Series. The question: What is the difference between the Fourier Transform and Fourier Series?
Both tools split a signal into sine waves. The Fourier series is for signals that repeat forever.
Their sine waves sit only at the repeat frequency and its whole-number multiples, so the spectrum (the list of frequencies present) is a set of separate lines.
The Fourier transform is for signals that do not repeat, such as a single pulse. Its spectrum is a smooth curve covering every frequency.
The two are linked: the lines of a repeating pulse sit on the smooth curve of the single pulse.
A choir holding a steady chord gives a few distinct notes: a set of lines. A single drum hit has no steady pitch, and its energy spreads smoothly across many frequencies.
Repeat the drum hit and the spread breaks into lines. Make the gaps longer and the lines pack closer until they blend back into the smooth curve.
The dots are the Fourier series amplitudes at harmonics of 1 kilohertz; the dashed envelope is the transform of a single 0. 25 milliseconds pulse.
The pulse train samples the envelope every 1 over T .
The nulls at multiples of 1 over tau equals 4 kilohertz are the harmonics where the pulse width equals a whole number of cycles, so the harmonic integrates to zero.
(The DC value is 0. 25 volts, not shown.)
Periodic: repeating the same shape every period T . Fundamental: the lowest frequency, 1 over T . Harmonic: a whole-number multiple of the fundamental.
Amplitude: the peak height of a sine wave. Aperiodic: not repeating, such as a single pulse. for its transform. Duty cycle: the fraction of each period the signal is high.
A square wave that swings between +A and minus A, high half the time, has only odd harmonics. Their amplitudes are 4 amps ÷ (nπ): about 1. 27 amps for the fundamental, 0.
42 amps for the third and 0. 25 amps for the fifth. Now a 0 to 1 volts pulse train at 1 kilohertz with 0. 25 milliseconds pulses, a 25% duty cycle. The average is 0. 25 volts.
The first harmonics are about 0. 45 volts, 0. 32 volts and 0. 15 volts. The 4th harmonic, at 4 kilohertz (1 ÷ the pulse width), is zero. That is the whole idea.
"Fourier series is for periodic signals: a sum of sinusoids at the fundamental and its harmonics, so the spectrum is discrete lines.
The Fourier transform is for aperiodic signals and gives a continuous spectrum.

They're connected: a periodic signal's series coefficients are samples of one period's transform, spaced 1 over T apart, and as the period goes to infinity the lines merge into the continuous transform.
The FFT treats a finite record as one period."
